paras: The Fernandina disturbance of July 1881 was a street conflict in Fernandina, Florida, on July 4, 1881, in which a Black man was wounded during an arrest or a quarrel with a policeman's family, and a Black crowd then threatened the men held responsible. The mayor called out the local military and the governor sent troops from Jacksonville, and a wire brief carried the story to papers from New York to Dallas as a threatened riot.

The town was crowded with Black excursionists for the Fourth of July holiday. According to passengers who reached Savannah from Florida, the trouble began in a barroom quarrel between a Black man and a white man that moved into the street and drew a crowd.

Policeman Wimberly was caught up in the tumult, escaped the crowd, and was joined by his brother and father, who were reported to have stabbed Levi Young, a Black man with whom the policeman had had "a difficulty." A Jacksonville dispatch gave a shorter version, saying a Black man who resisted arrest was shot and "painfully, though not mortally, wounded." The Weekly Floridian likewise traced the crowd's anger to "the arrest of one of their number."

In the Savannah account, the crowd followed the Wimberlys toward their home and threatened to burn the house. The three men were then taken to the jail, and the crowd threatened to set fire to it and lynch them. Mayor Starke called on the Fernandina military and telegraphed Governor Bloxham, who ordered out the Jacksonville Infantry; the troops were quartered at Lyceum Hall and a guard was placed around the jail.

After the troops arrived, the Savannah paper reported, there were no further fears for the jail or the prisoners, and it predicted that the ringleaders of the mob would be "dealt with severely." The Floridian instead credited "individuals of their own color" with quieting the crowd. No report of charges against the Wimberlys, an inquiry into Young's wounding, or arrests of crowd leaders appears in the coverage.

Outside Florida the episode reached readers through a brief Jacksonville wire dispatch printed on July 6 by the Chicago Daily Tribune under "Resisted Arrest," by the New York Sun as "Almost a Riot Over the Arrest of a Negro," by the Dallas Daily Herald and by the National Republican, which misprinted the wound as "fatally, though not mortally." That version named no one, gave resistance as the reason for the shooting, and presented the Black excursionists as the danger.

The Savannah Morning News, the only paper to name Levi Young or the Wimberlys, called the affair a "disgraceful riot" that left the town "at the mercy of a drunken mob," while still reporting that the policeman's relatives had done the stabbing. A week later the Tallahassee Weekly Floridian declined to give details "for want of space and inclination" and complained that "sensational telegrams calling it a riot" had been sent out of the state. No Black-press account appears in the coverage.

The accounts disagree on how the Black man was hurt: the wire says he was shot while resisting arrest, while the Savannah report says Levi Young was stabbed by the policeman's brother and father. Neither is a local or sworn account, and the Savannah version rests on what arriving passengers reported.

reader.title: Fernandina disturbance of July 1881
bases: The wire says a Black man was shot while resisting arrest and the Floridian ties the trouble to an arrest (A2, A7), while the Savannah account says a policeman's brother and father were reported to have stabbed Levi Young, colored (A5); in every version the violence against a Black man came from a policeman or his family, not a mob.

Three independent reports, the Jacksonville wire, the Savannah passengers' account and the Weekly Floridian, agree that on July 4 a row at Fernandina involving the arrest or wounding of a Black man led to a threatened outbreak and a call for the military (A2, A5, A7), though they differ on how he was hurt and by whom.

accounts.label: Jacksonville wire report
accounts.gist: A Black man resisting arrest was shot and painfully but not mortally wounded; with the town full of Black excursionists a riot was threatened until the militia restored quiet.

accounts.label: Passengers from Florida (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: A barroom quarrel between a Black man and a white man spilled into the street; Policeman Wimberly's brother and father were reported to have stabbed Levi Young, and a Black crowd threatened to burn their house and then to fire the jail and lynch them.

accounts.label: Weekly Floridian
accounts.gist: A row between a white man and a Black man led a Black crowd, angered by the arrest of one of their number, to seek vengeance on the police; they were quieted by Black residents, and the riot telegrams were 'sensational'.

framing.detail: The wire brief ran under 'Resisted Arrest', 'Almost a Riot Over the Arrest of a Negro' and 'A Riot quesched [quenched]', treating the shooting as justified by resistance and the Black crowd as the threat.
The Savannah Morning News called it a 'disgraceful riot' by a 'drunken mob' of Black people while also reporting that the policeman's relatives stabbed Levi Young.
The Weekly Floridian declined to give details 'for want of space and inclination' and called the riot telegrams 'sensational', crediting Black residents with restoring peace.

The National Republican's 'fatally' is a misprint of the same wire text.
